original_metadata.title: Hepatic impairment and CYP3A4 inhibition: simulated exposure of the fictional drug Beispielin

document_metadata.title: Hepatic impairment and CYP3A4 inhibition: simulated exposure of the fictional drug Beispielin
authors: John Doe, Example Institute of Pharmacometrics
Jane Doe, Example Institute of Pharmacometrics
document_metadata.abstract: Beispielin is a fictional drug that is metabolised almost completely by CYP3A4 in the liver. We simulated its exposure in patients with hepatic impairment and during co-administration of a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor. Both situations increase exposure, and their combination leads to the largest change, which argues for avoiding the inhibitor in hepatic impairment.

elements.text: Drugs that depend on a single metabolic enzyme are sensitive to everything that changes the activity of that enzyme. For CYP3A4 substrates, liver disease and inhibiting comedication are the two most common causes of increased exposure, and drug-drug interaction studies are therefore part of every development programme.

A whole-body PBPK model of Beispielin was combined with a virtual population of patients with mild, moderate and severe hepatic impairment, graded by a fictional severity score. Hepatic impairment was represented by reduced liver volume, reduced hepatic blood flow and lower CYP3A4 abundance. The inhibitor was modelled as a reversible competitive inhibitor of CYP3A4 with a fictional inhibition constant.

In severe hepatic impairment the area under the curve of Beispielin increased 3.1-fold, and co-administration of the inhibitor increased it 4.5-fold in subjects with normal liver function. The combination of both led to a 9-fold increase.
Unlike the liver, the kidney contributes less than five percent to the elimination of Beispielin, so kidney impairment was not considered further in this simulation.

The simulations suggest that the inhibitor should be avoided in patients with moderate or severe hepatic impairment. The prediction rests on fictional enzyme abundances and would need verification with clinical interaction data.
